title: Crime scene cleaning
estimatedMinutesNote: Estimated, not verified. Rule: learner text 3631 words / 100 per minute + 3 min per knowledge check (12) + 5 min allowance, rounded to nearest 5, minimum 15.

instruction.heading: Module authority and restricted work
instruction.body: This module is training content. It does not grant authority to enter a scene, to take control of a scene, to disturb or remove anything that may be evidence, or to carry out regulated remediation, transport or disposal. Completing this lesson does not give a licence, certificate, forensic clearance or any other authority. Police, coronial and other official authority controls many scenes, and their release must be obtained in writing before any work starts, whether or not the property owner or manager agrees. Insurer, property-owner and employer authority is also needed where it applies. Some of the work described here is restricted to licensed, authorised or specially trained people. Where you cannot identify who holds the authority, stop and refer.

instruction.heading: 1. Scope and referral boundaries
instruction.body: The intake coordinator's first task is to classify the request. It may be general cleaning, specialist remediation, waste transport or a possible evidence-controlled scene, and the classification decides who must be involved next. A client request, an insurance work order or a set of keys does not establish authority to start. Record the requesting party, the party that controls the property, the location, the uncertainty about what happened there, and every authority that still has to be confirmed. Before any step, confirm the site context, the authority and the documented approval. Separate what has been observed from what has been assumed, record each uncertainty and identify which actions need a competent supervisor or a licensed specialist. Use the employer's written plan and the local requirements. Finish by documenting the decision, the named reviewer, the exclusions and the handover. Competence is never inferred from a written quiz. In a scenario where a property manager presses a worker to clean a flat at once, with no police release on file, the worker holds the job and documents the reason. The coordinator lists the role-and-authority gaps and issues a written hold notice listing the missing evidence.

instruction.heading: 2. Scene release and evidence preservation
instruction.body: Police or coronial release of a scene is a separate matter from the owner's permission and from the employer's health-and-safety authorisation. All three must be considered, and none of them replaces the others. Treat photographs, found property and any unexpected physical evidence as controlled. Do not move them, do not speculate about what they mean, and do not alter the area around them. Record the authority that issued the release and the exact boundaries it covers. If a contractor is given a general building access code while an investigation is still open in one room, the code does not reach that room. Suspend work where the release is unclear, where a potentially relevant object has been found, or where a boundary is unmarked, and notify the authorised lead. In training, annotate a fictional floor plan with the zones that are unavailable for entry and the route for escalating any evidence-preservation question.

instruction.heading: 3. Consent, dignity and privacy
instruction.body: Traumatic incidents involve real people, bereavement and highly sensitive information. Limit personal details to what the operational task needs, protect photographs and records, and use consent to define access and the scope of service. Workers must not photograph the scene or share images for social media, training examples or promotion. A respectful point of contact should be named for the family, the occupants and the property party. When a neighbour asks a cleaner for photographs and incident details after a death, the cleaner does not provide them. The request goes to the designated manager, who decides what, if anything, can be disclosed and to whom. In training, draft a privacy-safe client update, a minimal-data intake form and an access-control decision, using fictional details only.

instruction.heading: 4. Exposure pathways and occupational controls
instruction.body: Treat unknown blood, body fluids and contaminated surfaces as exposure hazards until they have been assessed under the employer's plan. The presence, scale and location of the hazard can be uncertain, including on materials and behind fixtures, and a site report may describe staining on flooring or a damaged wall with an unknown history. Recognise the plausible exposure routes: contact with broken skin, splashes to the eyes, nose or mouth, puncture, and inhalation where aerosols or dust are produced. Do not diagnose infection from appearance. Verify worker training, the occupational exposure controls and the incident procedure for the specific environment before any task begins. Stop any uncontrolled contact, any task that produces aerosols, and any work that lacks an approved exposure-control plan. In training, mark on a diagram the plausible exposure routes, the uncertainty areas and the specialist evidence that would be required.

instruction.heading: 5. Sharps and concealed hazards
instruction.body: Needles, scalpels, broken glass and concealed metal fragments may be present even where a room appears clear. A worker who sees a point of metal through a rubbish bag during a preliminary visual survey must not press, open or reach into the bag. Search and removal must be carried out by trained personnel under the site-specific procedure, and never by hand exploration of upholstery, waste bags or blind spaces. Establish the condition of any sharps container and whether disposal has been authorised before anything is moved. Isolate the item, mark the no-touch boundary, withdraw the people nearby and refer the matter to authorised staff. In training, run an inert mock scene to label no-touch boundaries, withdrawal routes and the sharps escalation chain, using props that contain no real sharp.

instruction.heading: 6. PPE assessment and doffing boundaries
instruction.body: PPE is selected from a documented hazard assessment for the specific task. It is not chosen from a one-size-fits-all kit or from appearance. Check product compatibility, the training held by each worker, the fit requirements where a respirator is needed, the limitations of each item and the boundary between clean and contaminated areas. Incorrect removal can transfer contamination onto the worker and beyond, so removal is taught and assessed by a supervisor using clean training equipment and no infectious substance. A new worker who offers to wear ordinary gloves and a disposable mask for an unidentified incident scene is not yet equipped for the job. Do not enter until the responsible qualified person has approved the PPE and verified the worker's competence. In training, compare anonymised hazard cards with permitted PPE decisions and practise a supervised, inert doffing evaluation.

instruction.heading: 7. Containment and contamination zoning
instruction.body: Clean, restricted, support and possibly contaminated zones should be defined only after a site assessment. Consider how people, waste and tools will move, and keep the approach practical for rooms, stairwells and shared areas. A zoning drawing is a planning tool. It does not prove environmental clearance. A shared hallway may have been used to move contaminated belongings, so its status must be reassessed rather than assumed. Unexpected spread, including migration outside the approved boundary or uncontrolled public access, requires a new assessment and an escalation. In training, mark a fictional floor plan with stop points, access controls and a documented reassessment trigger.

instruction.heading: 8. Surface and porous material decisions
instruction.body: Hard non-porous surfaces, porous fabrics, absorbent building materials and electronic devices cannot be assumed to accept the same cleaning method. Material damage, incomplete penetration and manufacturer compatibility all matter. The authorised remediation specialist decides whether a material is retained, removed, isolated or investigated further. A visibly clean appearance is not proof of decontamination. When a client asks for a stained mattress and nearby electronic devices to be returned to use straight away, the answer is no. Those items stay out of use until the required specialist evidence exists. In training, build a keep, quarantine or refer decision sheet for mock materials and record the unresolved basis for each decision.

instruction.heading: 9. Waste identification and chain of custody
instruction.body: Waste may fall into infectious, clinical, hazardous or municipal classes depending on the location and the source. The classification governs packaging, transport and disposal. A cleaning certificate does not create permission to transport waste. Record every change of custody, the authorised carrier and the supporting manifest, and do not invent a universal waste code. Potentially infectious waste must be kept apart from evidential objects. A contractor who suggests putting unidentified contaminated material into ordinary building rubbish is proposing something that must not happen. Do not bag suspect regulated waste for ordinary disposal, transport it or relabel it without authorisation. In training, create a simulated waste decision log that identifies the classification questions, the approval owners and the handover evidence.

instruction.heading: 10. Equipment controls and decontamination limits
instruction.body: Equipment and reusable supplies can carry contaminants between work zones, vehicles and future clients. Choose reusable or disposable items only through an approved work procedure, and confirm the manufacturer's instructions before any cleaning process is used. Dedicated transport containment and separate storage prevent cross-use. A team that proposes using the same vacuum on a domestic job directly after an incident job has not yet met the control, and the equipment must be quarantined until its exposure history is known and specialist direction is given. In training, develop an equipment-use eligibility register and a mock isolation and tag-out record, and identify any decontamination claim that still needs validation.

instruction.heading: 11. Exposure incidents and worker wellbeing
instruction.body: Exposure incidents need immediate reporting, followed by the employer's medical evaluation and any public-health response the procedure requires. Workers may also experience stress, grief or an acute reaction after a traumatic site. Offer confidential support and make clear that a worker can stop work. Never require a worker to recount graphic detail beyond what the operation needs. A worker who reports a possible puncture injury and feels pressured to finish the shift must stop the task, activate the exposure-incident protocol and be referred for clinical assessment. In training, practise a simulated incident notification that records the time, the exposure details, the immediate escalation and the wellbeing referral.

instruction.heading: 12. Documentation, verification and handover
instruction.body: A handover must separate the tasks performed, the independent checks made, the hazards still outstanding and the work expressly excluded. Photographs and disposal receipts are kept only with permission and under controlled retention. Do not claim forensic clearance, biological safety, zero pathogens or habitability unless a competent authority has verified that specific basis. A client who demands a certificate that a building is completely safe after limited specialist work is asking for something the work does not support. Withhold the unsupported claim, escalate the unresolved hazards and make no return-to-use recommendation until the authority has decided. Record the sign-off and the owner of the next review. In training, prepare a scope-limited completion report with separate fields for evidence, exclusions, unresolved issues and referrals.

instruction.heading: Stop-work and referral rules for this module
instruction.body: Stop and refer whenever the scene release is unclear, the applicable jurisdiction or the worker's authorisation is unknown, a potentially relevant object has been found, a sharp is present or suspected, a worker may have been exposed, the PPE has not been approved, a waste route is unauthorised, equipment has an unknown exposure history, or a party asks for a clearance or safety claim the work cannot support. Do not handle evidence or regulated material beyond your remit. A stop-work decision is a correct decision and is recorded as one.

procedure: Stop before any entry. Confirm in writing the scene release, the scope of the authority that gave it and any boundary it sets.
If a potentially relevant object is seen, do not touch, move, open or photograph it. Isolate the area and notify the authorised lead.
Record the issuing authority, the released boundaries, the people present and the time.
If anyone may have been exposed, end the activity and activate the exposure-incident protocol and clinical referral.
Do not disclose personal details or take images. Refer all requests to the designated manager.
Refer waste, specialist decisions on porous or electronic items, and any clearance question to the authorised party.
Record the decision, the referral and the next competent reviewer in the job file.
Issue a scope-limited handover that states the work done, the checks made, the exclusions and the unverified outcomes.

workedExamples.situation: A property manager pressures a worker to clean a flat immediately, but there is no police release on file.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What must the worker document, communicate and decide before any work proceeds?
workedExamples.reasoning: The worker identifies the unverified site facts and does not assume the scene has been released. The worker holds the job, records the reason, escalates to the designated supervisor and waits for the written release and the approved plan. The decision and the reviewer are documented.

workedExamples.situation: A contractor has been given a general building access code while an investigation is still open in one room.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Does the code allow entry to that room?
workedExamples.reasoning: No. A general access code does not release a room under investigation. The room is excluded, the boundary is marked, work in that area is suspended and the authorised lead is notified.

workedExamples.situation: A worker sees a point of metal through a rubbish bag during a visual survey.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What must the worker do with the bag?
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not press, open or reach into the bag. Mark the no-touch boundary, withdraw nearby people and refer to trained, authorised staff under the site procedure.

workedExamples.situation: A client asks for a stained mattress and nearby electronic devices to be returned to use straight away.
workedExamples.reasoning: Decline. A visibly clean appearance is not proof of decontamination. The items remain out of use until the authorised specialist has made a decision on retaining, removing or isolating them, and the required evidence exists.

workedExamples.situation: A client demands a certificate that a building is completely safe after limited specialist work.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What can be written in the handover?
workedExamples.reasoning: Only what was done, what was checked, what remains outstanding and what was excluded. The coordinator withholds the unsupported safety claim and makes no return-to-use recommendation while the authority has not decided.

commonErrors.error: Treating the owner's or manager's permission as police or coronial release.
commonErrors.prevention: Obtain and record the written release from the controlling authority. Owner permission is a separate matter.

commonErrors.error: Moving or tidying objects that might be evidence.
commonErrors.prevention: Leave them in place, isolate the area and notify the authorised lead.

commonErrors.error: Sharing photographs or incident details with neighbours, family or social media.
commonErrors.prevention: Refer every request to the designated manager. Take no images without authority.

commonErrors.error: Using ordinary gloves and a disposable mask for an unidentified incident scene.
commonErrors.prevention: PPE is approved against the hazard assessment and the worker's training before entry.

commonErrors.error: Putting suspect material into ordinary building rubbish or a private vehicle.
commonErrors.prevention: Classify the waste first and use only the authorised carrier, with custody records kept.

commonErrors.error: Reusing a vacuum or other tool straight after an incident job.
commonErrors.prevention: Quarantine the equipment until its history is known and specialist direction is given.

commonErrors.error: Returning a stained mattress or electronics to use because they look clean.
commonErrors.prevention: Keep them out of use until the authorised specialist decides on each item.

commonErrors.error: Pressing on, or waiting until the shift ends, after a possible puncture or splash.
commonErrors.prevention: Stop, activate the exposure-incident protocol and arrange clinical assessment.

commonErrors.error: Issuing a certificate that the building or room is safe or free of pathogens.
commonErrors.prevention: Claim only what was verified. Refer clearance to a competent authority.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: This module does not grant authority to enter, control or work on any scene, or to handle evidence. Completing it does not give a licence, certificate, forensic clearance or police authorisation.
Police, coronial and other official release must be obtained in writing before work starts. The release covers only the boundaries it names. Owner, manager or insurer permission does not replace it.
Some work described here, including regulated waste transport, sharps collection and specialist decontamination, is restricted to licensed or specially authorised operators.
The US and UK sources are reference only and are not Australian law. Some are healthcare-setting references, and the source research states they do not extend to crime-scene clearance.
Exposure, PPE and waste decisions follow the employer's plan and the applicable local rules. This lesson does not replace them.
No product, dilution, contact time, quantity or processing method is given. Drug-related and chemical processing are outside this module.
Dignity and privacy duties apply to all records and communications. Do not photograph, publish or share scene details.

summary: A request is classified before anything else. Access, remediation authority and police or coronial release are three different things.
Do not move, photograph or speculate about potential evidence. Isolate and notify.
Protect the privacy and dignity of the people involved. Refer every request for information.
Treat unknown material as hazardous. Use the approved exposure-control plan and PPE chosen for the task.
Never handle an unidentified sharp. Mark, withdraw and escalate.
Zones are planning tools, not proof of clearance. Reassess when anything moves outside the boundary.
Porous and electronic items need specialist decisions. A clean look is not proof.
Waste is classified and handled only by authorised operators, with custody recorded.
Report exposures at once and offer wellbeing support. Workers can stop work.
Hand over only what was done, and withhold clearance claims that the authority has not made.

officialReferences.title: Duties of a person conducting a business or undertaking (PCBU)
officialReferences.covers: Confirms the PCBU duty to workers and others so far as reasonably practicable, and refers to the hierarchy of control. It does not say PPE is a last resort. Check your state or territory WHS regulator for the adopted law. Publisher: Safe Work Australia.

officialReferences.title: Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Control of Infection in Healthcare (2019), CD34
officialReferences.pageDate: no page date shown; document dated 2019 (CD34)
officialReferences.covers: Read: sections on environmental cleaning, spills, hand hygiene, standard precautions and sharps. Not read: section 3.1.4 (reprocessing), 3.1.7 (waste), 4.1.2 (roles) and Appendix 6.1 (frequencies). Check those in the full PDF. Publisher: National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC).

officialReferences.title: Managing spills of blood and body fluids and substances
officialReferences.covers: Read via summary tool (WebFetch). The page is written for healthcare settings and also covers public locations, community premises and wet areas. It says to clear up the spilled material before cleaning the area, to use PPE for all cleaning and dispose of it or send it for cleaning afterwards, and to use leak-proof bags and containers for waste. It says sodium hypochlorite is generally unnecessary for spills. Publisher: Victorian Department of Health.

officialReferences.title: Forensic cleaning services guidelines
officialReferences.pageDate: Reviewed on 17/11/2025 (no published or updated date shown)
officialReferences.covers: Read via summary tool (WebFetch). Says WorkSafe Victoria can fund forensic (trauma) cleaning after a work-related death at a worker's or family member's home, for deaths on or after 6 August 2025, and that providers must be registered with WorkSafe and hold a recognised forensic or trauma cleaning certification and the required insurance. Does not describe PPE, waste handling or a government licence for this work, and does not confirm any authority to enter or clean a scene. Publisher: WorkSafe Victoria.

knowledgeChecks.question: A property manager wants a flat cleaned today, but no police release is on file. What should the worker do?
options: Hold the job, document the reason and escalate for the written release and approved plan.
Start, because the property manager has the keys and has asked for the work to begin today
Clean the living areas now and leave the rest for later, since the job is still under way

knowledgeChecks.question: A general building access code has been given to a contractor. An investigation is still open in one room. What does the code allow?
options: Entry to every room, because the code is general and the contractor was given it for the job
Nothing about the open room. The code does not release it, so it stays excluded and the lead is notified.
Entry to the open room only if the contractor is careful and wears the right protective gear

knowledgeChecks.question: A neighbour asks a cleaner for photographs and incident details after a death. What is correct?
options: Send the photographs, because the neighbour is concerned about the property
Give the basic details but no photographs, since the neighbour lives close by
Refer the request to the designated manager, who decides what can be disclosed.

knowledgeChecks.question: A worker sees a point of metal through a rubbish bag. What should the worker do?
options: Mark the no-touch boundary, withdraw nearby people and refer to trained, authorised staff.
Open the bag carefully to see what it is, so the crew knows what they are dealing with
Press on the bag to check the shape of the object, since that is a gentle way to test it

knowledgeChecks.question: A new worker offers to wear ordinary gloves and a disposable mask for an unidentified incident scene. What is the response?
options: Accept, because the worker is keen to help and has done some general cleaning before
Do not enter until the responsible qualified person approves the PPE and verifies competence.
Allow entry if the worker signs a form that says they accept the risk and the job is urgent

knowledgeChecks.question: The site report describes staining on flooring and a damaged wall with an unknown history. What is the first decision?
options: Treat the staining as harmless because it looks dry and the damage on the wall is old and cosmetic
Assume the risk is limited to the visible area only, since the rest of the room looks fine today
Treat it as an exposure hazard until assessed under the employer's plan, with no uncontrolled contact.

knowledgeChecks.question: Two zones on a site plan look clean. What does the zoning drawing establish?
options: A planning tool only. It does not prove environmental clearance, so reassessment is needed if spread is suspected.
Environmental clearance for both zones, since the drawing shows they have been cleaned and checked by the team
That the zones can be used by the public straight away, since the clean areas are open to visitors now and staff

knowledgeChecks.question: A client asks for a stained mattress and nearby electronic devices to be returned to use immediately. What is the response?
options: Return them, because they look clean and the surfaces show no sign of any contamination at all
Keep them out of use until the authorised specialist has decided on each item and the required evidence exists.
Clean them with a household product and return them, since the product removes everything visible

knowledgeChecks.question: A contractor proposes putting unidentified contaminated material into ordinary building rubbish. What is correct?
options: Do it, because it is quicker than arranging a carrier and the building bins are collected daily at the site
Do it if the bags are tied tightly and placed in the bin with the lid closed on the day of the job at the site
Do not bag or dispose of suspect regulated waste without authorisation. Classify it first and use the authorised carrier.

knowledgeChecks.question: A team proposes using the same vacuum on a domestic job straight after an incident job. What is correct?
options: Quarantine the equipment until its exposure history is known and specialist direction is given.
Use it, because it has been cleaned and it looks ready to go for the next job today
Use it only if the job is short and the next client does not mind any dust in the room

knowledgeChecks.question: A worker reports a possible puncture injury and feels pressured to finish the shift. What is correct?
options: Finish the shift and report at the end, since the wound is minor and can wait until then
Stop the task, activate the exposure-incident protocol and arrange clinical assessment.
Bandage the wound and continue if the bleeding has stopped, since the cut is small

knowledgeChecks.question: A client demands a certificate that a building is completely safe after limited specialist work. What is correct?
options: Issue the certificate to keep the client satisfied and avoid any further argument on site
Issue the certificate with a note that the building is safe for adults only and not for children
Withhold the unsupported claim, escalate the unresolved hazards and make no return-to-use recommendation.
